## API-01 Login endpoint is rate limited (429 + Retry-After)

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-307, CWE-770 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Without per-account and per-IP limits on login, signup, password reset and OTP verify, attackers can credential-stuff accounts and brute-force 6-digit codes. Custom routes that check a secret themselves get none of Supabase Auth's built-in limits, and in-memory counters reset per serverless instance.

### Build rule

Use Supabase Auth's built-in endpoints where possible and keep its limits on. For any custom route or Server Action that checks a password, OTP, reset or invite code, enforce a shared-store limiter (Upstash @upstash/ratelimit sliding window, or a Vercel WAF rate-limit rule on the path), never an in-memory Map. Key it by both client IP and normalized target account, e.g. 5 per 15 min per account and 20 per 15 min per IP. Return 429 with a Retry-After header. Apply the limit inside the handler, not only in middleware (see NEXT checks). Do not reveal whether the account exists. Key IPs correctly (API-14).

### Proof test

1. Run the CLI with --rate-limit-path set to the login endpoint of the user's own site, e.g. /api/auth/login. Without a path the CLI uses a same-origin POST login form found by the crawl (one password field; a page or action that names login, sign-in, session or auth, and never sign-up, register or reset), filling only the user and password fields with fake values. With neither the check reports manual.
2. The CLI sends up to N requests (default 30, max 60) with fake credentials that match no real account, and stops at the first sign of throttling.
3. Pass: a 429 with Retry-After appears within N requests; the report gives the attempt number.
4. Warning: throttling of another kind, reported with the attempt number where it began: a 429 without Retry-After, a change to another error status (400, 403, 423, 503...), or limit words that the first answer did not have ("too many", "locked", "captcha"...). Also a warning: every answer stayed the same ("no limit observed up to N"), because many limits sit above 30 attempts. A detected form that refuses the first attempt with 400 or 403 (often a CSRF token) is reported as manual.
5. Manual follow-up: with an owned test account, confirm the correct password is also refused or challenged during the lockout.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10)
- [Supabase Auth rate limits](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/rate-limits)
- [Vercel WAF rate limiting](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/rate-limiting)
- [Upstash Ratelimit overview](https://upstash.com/docs/redis/sdks/ratelimit-ts/overview)

## API-02 Errors do not leak stack traces or internals

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-209, CWE-215 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Handlers that return err.message or err.stack, or forward Supabase/PostgREST errors verbatim (details, hint, table and constraint names, SQL), hand attackers a map of the schema and code, and confirm when a probe hit something. Upstream API errors can echo keys or internal URLs.

### Build rule

Route every route handler and Server Action through one handleError() helper: log the full error server-side with a request id, return { error: "Something went wrong", id } with the right status. Map validation errors to field-level messages without echoing internals. Never return Supabase error.details, error.hint or error.message to clients. Run with NODE_ENV=production and no debug flags. Source maps belong to NEXT-02.

### Proof test

1. The CLI requests a random path that does not exist on the user's own site.
2. It sends a malformed JSON body to a random path under /api/, and to the login endpoint (--rate-limit-path, or the login form found by the crawl, as in API-01).
3. Pass: no response contains stack frames, file paths (/var/task, node_modules, C:\), SQL or PGRST text, or framework internals, and at least one answer is an error other than 404/405, so a handler's error path actually ran.
4. Fail: any of those markers appears in a response body.
5. Manual: only not-found or wrong-method answers came back. They come from the router and do not prove what a handler shows when it fails.
6. Manual follow-up: send malformed JSON, wrong types and an invalid UUID to each real API route and check the same markers.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API8 Security Misconfiguration)](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10)
- [Next.js: Error Handling](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling)
- [OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## API-03 SMS and OTP sending is capped against toll fraud

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-799, CWE-770 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

Any endpoint that sends an SMS (phone OTP, "text me a link", callback request) can be scripted to send to premium-rate ranges, billing the site owner per message. Email-sending endpoints have the same shape. Limiting per phone number alone fails because numbers rotate. Twitter limited SMS 2FA to paid users in 2023 citing this abuse.

### Build rule

Put a server-verified CAPTCHA (Turnstile or hCaptcha) before any SMS send. Rate-limit by IP, by session or user, by destination number, plus a global hourly cap per country prefix and a daily spend cap. Allowlist the destination countries you serve (Twilio Verify Geo Permissions or the Supabase SMS provider settings). Prefer Twilio Verify with Fraud Guard over raw Programmable SMS. Keep Supabase's project SMS cap low. Alert on send-volume spikes.

### Proof test

1. Use only a phone number the owner controls.
2. Request an OTP 6 times within 2 minutes against the user's own site.
3. Pass: the second request inside 60 s is rejected and by the fourth the endpoint returns 429; a request without a valid CAPTCHA token is rejected 400/403.
4. Fail: all 6 messages arrive.
5. Review config: a country allowlist and a global send cap exist. Never send to numbers the owner does not control.

### Sources

- [Twilio Verify SMS Fraud Guard](https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify/preventing-toll-fraud/sms-fraud-guard)
- [Twilio: SMS pumping protection options](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/developers/best-practices/sms-pumping-protection-options)
- [Supabase Auth rate limits](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/rate-limits)
- [NBC News: Twitter limits SMS 2FA to paid users](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/twitter-limit-use-text-messages-two-factor-authentication-paid-subscri-rcna71305)

## API-04 Input is schema-validated before use

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-20 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: nextjs, supabase

### Risk

Route handlers and Server Actions receive arbitrary JSON and FormData whatever the TypeScript types say. Passing the body straight into insert or update lets a client set role, is_admin, user_id, price or status. GitHub's 2012 mass-assignment bug (CVE-2012-2055) let a user add his key to the Rails organization.

### Build rule

Parse every route.ts, Server Action and [param] input with a zod schema using .strict(): allowlisted fields, bounded numbers, length-capped strings, enums for sort fields, z.string().uuid() for ids. Map validated input to an explicit object before insert, update or upsert; never pass body or formData spreads. Set user_id and owner server-side from the session. Protect privileged columns with RLS WITH CHECK and column grants (revoke update (role) on profiles from authenticated). Return DTOs, not raw rows. Reject wrong Content-Type and oversized bodies.

### Proof test

1. Sign in with the user's own test account.
2. Send wrong types to each write endpoint (a string where a number belongs, an array where a string belongs, a 100 KB string) and an unknown extra field.
3. Pass: 400 with a generic message, and the unknown field is dropped or rejected. Fail: 500, a stack trace, or the value stored.
4. Review: grep the repo for .insert(body, .update(await req.json()) and formData spreads; each needs a schema parse first.
Writing privileged columns (role, is_admin, plan) through an update is owned by ACCESS-05.

### Sources

- [Next.js: How to think about data security](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/data-security)
- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API3 BOPLA)](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10)
- [CVE-2012-2055 GitHub mass assignment](https://db.gcve.eu/vuln/fkie_cve-2012-2055)
- [OWASP Mass Assignment Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Mass_Assignment_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## API-05 User input never builds PostgREST filter strings

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-89, CWE-943 · Mode: assisted (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: supabase

### Risk

supabase-js .or(), .filter(), .not() and hand-built REST query strings treat , . : ( ) " as syntax. User text concatenated into them can add conditions or change which columns are compared, exposing or modifying rows when RLS is weak or the service-role key is used. CVE-2026-77071 in the n8n Supabase node matched every row this way.

### Build rule

Pass user values only as arguments to typed builder methods: .eq('id', id), .ilike('name', `%${q}%`). Never interpolate input into .or(), .filter(), .not(), select() column lists or order() column names. If .or() is unavoidable, validate input against a strict allowlist regex (e.g. ^[\p{L}\p{N} _-]{1,64}$) or quote it per PostgREST reserved-character rules. Take sort and column names from an enum. RLS must still bound every query (ACCESS checks); service-role code adds explicit ownership filters.

### Proof test

1. On the user's own app with seeded test data, submit benign search terms containing reserved characters: a,b then test) then x.y then a quote.
2. Pass: results equal a literal match (usually empty) or a 400 validation error.
3. Fail: a 500 with a PostgREST parse error (PGRST100) in the response, or more rows than a literal match returns.
4. Review: grep the repo for .or( and .filter( called with template literals or string concatenation.
5. Do not attempt to read other users' data.

### Sources

- [VulnCheck: n8n Supabase node PostgREST filter injection (CVE-2026-77071)](https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/n8n-before-postgrest-filter-injection-via-supabase)
- [SignalizeAI issue showing PostgREST filter injection from a search box](https://github.com/SignalizeAI/SignalizeAI-Website/issues/50)

## API-06 Webhooks verify signatures and reject replays

Severity: critical · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-345, CWE-290, CWE-294 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

A webhook route is a public URL. If it does not verify the signature over the raw body, anyone can POST a fake checkout.session.completed and get goods, credits or role upgrades. CVE-2026-21894: the n8n Stripe Trigger stored the signing secret but never checked it, so forged events ran workflows.

### Build rule

In the webhook route read await req.text() and pass it with the Stripe-Signature header to stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(raw, sig, secret); keep the default 300 s tolerance. Never call req.json() before verifying. Fail closed when the secret env var is missing. For other providers use their SDK verifier or an HMAC over the raw body compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual. Store processed event ids under a unique constraint and skip duplicates. Re-fetch the object from the provider before granting anything high value. Never put webhook secrets in NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars. Exclude webhook routes from auth middleware, not from verification.

### Proof test

1. Against the user's own webhook route in test mode, POST a well-formed Stripe-like event with no Stripe-Signature header.
2. POST it again with a garbage signature header, then with a header whose timestamp is 1 hour old.
3. Pass: all three return 400/401 and no side effect appears in the database or logs. Fail: 200 and the handler runs.
4. Positive control: stripe trigger checkout.session.completed with the Stripe CLI returns 200; resending the same event id from the Dashboard is processed once.

### Sources

- [Stripe: Webhook signatures](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks/signature)
- [GHSA-jf52-3f2h-h9j5 / CVE-2026-21894 n8n Stripe Trigger missing signature check](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-jf52-3f2h-h9j5)
- [Vercel: x-vercel-signature verification](https://vercel.com/docs/headers/request-headers#x-vercel-signature)

## API-07 Database functions are not over-exposed or injectable

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-89, CWE-250, CWE-285 · Mode: review · Stacks: supabase

### Risk

supabase.rpc() calls Postgres functions over the public REST API, and by default any role can run them, including anon. SECURITY DEFINER functions bypass RLS, so a missing ownership check or unset search_path becomes an authorization hole. Functions that concatenate arguments into EXECUTE are injectable.

### Build rule

Prefer security invoker. If security definer is needed: set search_path = '', schema-qualify every table, check auth.uid() ownership in the body, and either move it to a non-exposed schema or revoke execute on function ... from public, anon and grant only to authenticated. In dynamic SQL use EXECUTE format('... %I ...', col) USING val, never ||. Validate rpc arguments with zod in the app too. Run the Supabase security advisor, which flags mutable search_path. Table RLS belongs to ACCESS checks.

### Proof test

1. In the database, list functions in exposed schemas with prosecdef = true and no search_path in proconfig. Pass: none, or each sets search_path. Fail: any definer function without it.
2. Grep migrations for EXECUTE with || concatenation. Pass: none, or each uses format() with %I/%L or a parameter. Fail: any concatenated SQL.
3. Optional, with two owned test accounts: call a definer function as account A with account B's id. Pass: empty or 403. Fail: B's data.
Whether definer functions and views bypass RLS, and EXECUTE grants to anon, are owned by ACCESS-06.

### Sources

- [Supabase: Database functions](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/functions)
- [PostgreSQL: PL/pgSQL executing dynamic commands](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/plpgsql-statements.html)

## API-08 Server-side URL fetches cannot reach internal addresses

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-918 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

Features that fetch a user-supplied URL server-side (link previews, import from URL, avatar by URL, outgoing webhook tests, next/image with broad remotePatterns) can be pointed at cloud metadata, localhost admin ports or private services. Redirects and DNS rebinding defeat hostname checks done before the fetch. Capital One's 2019 breach began with SSRF to EC2 metadata; Next.js has shipped SSRF fixes (CVE-2024-34351, CVE-2026-94483).

### Build rule

Keep next patched. In next.config images.remotePatterns list exact trusted hostnames plus pathname; no ** hostnames. For any server-side fetch of a user URL: allow only https, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, ULA and metadata ranges (IPv4, IPv6 and mapped forms), connect to the resolved IP, disable redirects or re-validate each hop, set a short timeout and a maximum response size, and never return raw upstream bodies or errors. Prefer a domain allowlist when the feature allows it. Run fetchers without cloud credentials in env.

### Proof test

1. On the user's own app's URL-taking feature, submit http://127.0.0.1/, http://169.254.169.254/, http://[::1]/ and http://localhost:3000/.
2. Submit a URL on a request-catcher the owner controls that redirects to 127.0.0.1.
3. Pass: all are rejected with 400 before any outbound connection; the catcher sees no follow-up. Fail: 200 with content, or response time/body shows an internal fetch.
4. The Next.js image optimizer (/_next/image) allow list is owned by NEXT-11.
5. Do not probe anyone else's network.

### Sources

- [Assetnote: Next.js Server Actions SSRF (CVE-2024-34351)](https://www.assetnote.io/resources/research/advisory-next-js-ssrf-cve-2024-34351)
- [GHSA-cjq9-62q9-8jv4 / CVE-2026-94483 Next.js Image Optimization SSRF](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-cjq9-62q9-8jv4)
- [OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [Wiz: Capital One breach (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/20250716150520/https://threats.wiz.io/all-incidents/capital-one-breach)

## API-09 List endpoints cap page size and query cost

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-770, CWE-400 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

Endpoints that take ?limit= or range() from the client, or select('*') without a limit, let one request dump a table or run expensive queries. Supabase caps responses at 1,000 rows by default, a setting developers often raise.

### Build rule

Validate paging with zod: limit = z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20). Use keyset (cursor) pagination on an indexed column and reject unknown sort columns. Keep Supabase Max rows at 1,000 or lower. Use count: 'estimated' or 'planned' on large tables. Set statement_timeout for the anon and authenticated roles. Cache public list endpoints.

### Proof test

1. Call each list endpoint on the user's own site once with ?limit=100000, ?limit=-1 and ?offset=99999999.
2. Call /rest/v1/<table>?select=* with a Range: 0-100000 header for a table the anon key may read.
3. Pass: at most the documented maximum rows, or 400.
4. Fail: thousands of rows, a timeout, or a 500.
5. Run each request once, not in a loop.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption)](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10)
- [Supabase JS reference: select (1,000 row default)](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/select)
- [PostgREST: Pagination and count](https://docs.postgrest.org/en/v12/references/api/pagination_count.html)

## API-10 File uploads are restricted by type and size

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-434, CWE-400 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

Trusting the client's filename or MIME type lets users upload HTML or SVG with script that is served from your origin (stored XSS), or huge files that exhaust storage and budget. CVE-2026-32753 (FreeScout) and CVE-2024-8029 (PrivateGPT) were both stored XSS through SVG uploads.

### Build rule

Set Supabase bucket allowed_mime_types and file_size_limit, and validate on the server by magic bytes, not extension. Generate object names server-side (<uid>/<uuid>.<ext>); never use user filenames as paths. Reject SVG, HTML and XML, or re-encode images (sharp). Serve user files from a separate origin such as the Supabase storage domain, with Content-Disposition: attachment for non-images and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Use private buckets and short-lived signed URLs for personal files. Restrict storage policies to the auth.uid() folder. Cap request body size (serverActions.bodySizeLimit).

### Proof test

1. With the user's own test account, upload a harmless SVG containing a script tag renamed to .png, then a file twice the stated size limit.
2. Pass: the type is checked from the content (magic bytes), not the name or the client's Content-Type, and the oversized file is rejected 413/400 before it is stored. Fail: either is stored.
3. Delete the test files afterwards.
How stored files are served (attachment, nosniff, separate origin) is owned by BROWSER-13.

### Sources

- [CVE-2026-32753 FreeScout SVG upload stored XSS](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-32753)
- [CVE-2024-8029 PrivateGPT SVG upload XSS](https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2024-8029/)
- [OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [GHSA-9g9p-9gw9-jx7f / CVE-2025-59471 Next.js image optimizer memory DoS](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-9g9p-9gw9-jx7f)

## API-11 Public forms verify CAPTCHA tokens on the server

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-799, CWE-602 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

Contact, signup, waitlist, booking and newsletter forms get spammed or used to send email from your domain, hurting reputation and cost. A Turnstile or hCaptcha widget without a server-side siteverify call gives no protection.

### Build rule

Every public form handler first POSTs the token to siteverify with the secret and remoteip, checks success, that hostname equals your domain and that action matches, and fails closed on network error. Enable Supabase Auth CAPTCHA for auth forms. Add a per-IP limiter (e.g. 5 per 10 min) and a honeypot field. Keep the secret out of NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars. Fix email recipients server-side and escape user content placed in outgoing email.

### Proof test

1. Submit the user's own form endpoint directly with no token, then with a dummy token, then replaying a token captured from one real browser submission.
2. Pass: all three are rejected 400/403 and no email or database row is created. Fail: any is accepted.
3. Send 10 valid-looking submissions in one minute. Pass: 429 after the configured limit.
4. Use Cloudflare's official test sitekeys on staging.

### Sources

- [Cloudflare Turnstile: Server-side validation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/server-side-validation/)
- [Supabase Auth CAPTCHA](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-captcha)

## API-12 LLM endpoints have auth, rate, token and spend caps

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-770, CWE-400, CWE-799 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

A public route that proxies to an LLM provider is a free model for anyone who finds it, and every call costs the owner money. Attackers send maximum-length prompts, ask for maximum output tokens, choose the most expensive model through a client parameter, or trigger agent loops. OWASP LLM10:2025 names this unbounded consumption.

### Build rule

Require a session or a server-verified CAPTCHA token on every LLM route. Rate-limit per user and per IP with a shared store, plus a daily per-user token budget. Cap input length and message count with zod, set max_tokens and the model server-side and ignore client values, set a request timeout and cap tool or agent iterations. Set provider spend limits and alerts, and use project-scoped keys kept in server env only.

### Proof test

1. Call the user's own LLM endpoint with no session and no CAPTCHA token. Pass: 401/403.
2. Send 25 tiny prompts in one minute. Pass: 429 at the configured limit.
3. Send a 200 KB prompt. Pass: 400/413 with no upstream call.
4. Send a request naming an expensive model and a huge max_tokens. Pass: logs or response metadata show server defaults were used.
5. Keep total calls under about 30 to limit the owner's cost.

### Sources

- [OWASP LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm102025-unbounded-consumption/)

## API-13 LLM output cannot exfiltrate data or trigger unapproved actions

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1427, CWE-200, CWE-77 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

When an LLM feature reads untrusted content and also has access to private data or tools, injected instructions can make it leak that data, often through a rendered markdown image or link whose URL carries the data out. Slack AI, Google Bard and Claude were all shown leaking data this way.

### Build rule

Treat model output as untrusted: render plain text or sanitized markdown with images and links disabled or limited to an allowlist of domains, and limit CSP img-src and connect-src to your own origins. Run retrieval and tools with the end user's Supabase JWT so RLS applies, never the service-role key, and scope retrieval to the current user or tenant. Require explicit user confirmation for high-impact tool calls (send email, delete, pay). Keep secrets out of system prompts. Log tool invocations.

### Proof test

1. In a test account on the user's own app, store a document containing a benign canary instruction asking the assistant to output an image whose URL points at an owner-controlled request-catcher.
2. Ask the feature to summarize that document.
3. Pass: no request reaches the catcher, no external image renders, no tool action runs. Fail: the catcher is hit or the image renders.
4. With two test accounts, ask account A's assistant about account B's canary text. Pass: no disclosure.

### Sources

- [OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)
- [PromptArmor: Data exfiltration from Slack AI via indirect prompt injection](https://promptarmor.com/resources/data-exfiltration-from-slack-ai-via-indirect-prompt-injection)
- [Simon Willison: Hacking Google Bard, from prompt injection to data exfiltration](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Nov/4/hacking-google-bard-from-prompt-injection-to-data-exfiltration/)
- [Embrace The Red: Anthropic fixes Claude data exfiltration via images](https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2023/anthropic-fixes-claude-data-exfiltration-via-images)
- [The Register: Slack AI prompt injection](https://www.theregister.com/2024/08/21/slack_ai_prompt_injection/)

## API-14 Rate limits key on a client IP that cannot be spoofed

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-348, CWE-290 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any

### Risk

A limiter keyed on the first X-Forwarded-For value, or on a client-sent X-Real-IP or CF-Connecting-IP, is bypassed by sending a new fake value per request. Keying on one proxy IP instead blocks every user at once. Vercel overwrites X-Forwarded-For; self-hosted setups do not unless configured.

### Build rule

On Vercel use ipAddress(request) from @vercel/functions or the x-vercel-forwarded-for / x-real-ip headers Vercel sets. Self-hosted: trust only the right-most IP added by your own proxy (configure the trusted proxy count), or a CDN header only when the origin accepts traffic solely from that CDN. Key auth limits by account as well as IP (API-01). If the IP is missing, fall back to one shared bucket.

### Proof test

1. Repeat the API-01 login test against the user's own site, adding a different X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP value from the 203.0.113.0/24 test range on every request.
2. Pass: 429 still appears at the same count as without the headers.
3. Fail: the limit never triggers.
4. Observe status codes only.

### Sources

- [Vercel: Request headers](https://vercel.com/docs/headers/request-headers)

## API-15 Prices and amounts are set on the server, never taken from the client

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-472, CWE-602 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

A checkout route that builds the Stripe Checkout Session or PaymentIntent from an `amount`, `price` or `unit_amount` the browser sent lets anyone pay one cent for anything by editing the request. A webhook that grants what the client asked for, rather than what was paid, has the same effect. OWASP lists this under insecure design and abuse of sensitive business flows.

### Build rule

The checkout route accepts only a product or price ID and a quantity. It looks up the price and currency on the server (a Stripe Price ID in `line_items[].price`, or a row in your own database), checks the quantity against allowed bounds, and ignores any amount, currency or discount field from the client. Never pass client values into `price_data.unit_amount` or a PaymentIntent `amount`. In the webhook, retrieve the Checkout Session with `line_items` expanded, check `payment_status`, and grant only what those paid line items cover. Webhook signatures are API-06.

### Proof test

1. In Stripe test mode, as your own test account, capture the request the site sends to start checkout.
2. Replay it with a changed amount, price, currency or discount field added or edited, and with a negative or huge quantity.
3. Open the resulting Checkout Session in the Stripe Dashboard (test mode) or retrieve it with the API.
Pass: the request is rejected, or the session uses the server's Price and an allowed quantity. Fail: the session total follows the edited value.
4. Review: grep the checkout code for `unit_amount`, `amount:` and `price_data` and confirm none takes a value from the request body.
Use test mode only; never complete a real payment.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0xa6-unrestricted-access-to-sensitive-business-flows/)
- [OWASP Top 10 2025: A06 Insecure Design](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A06_2025-Insecure_Design/)
- [Stripe docs: How products and prices work](https://docs.stripe.com/products-prices/how-products-and-prices-work)
- [Stripe docs: Fulfill orders (retrieve line_items, check payment_status)](https://docs.stripe.com/checkout/fulfillment)

## API-16 Authorization code fails closed on errors and missing config

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-636, CWE-703 · Mode: review · Stacks: any, nextjs, supabase

### Risk

An auth or permission helper that catches an exception and returns true, a check written as `if (user?.role === 'banned') deny` that lets every error through, or a secret compared against `process.env.X` when X is unset, all grant access when something goes wrong. Attackers trigger those error paths on purpose with malformed tokens, timeouts or odd input.

### Build rule

Write every permission check as allow-listing: grant only when the session is valid and the rule explicitly allows, and deny in every other branch, including `catch`. Read required secrets and config once at startup and refuse to start (or return 500 without acting) when one is missing. Never compare a request value against an env var that may be unset. Do not swallow errors from the session lookup, the database or the policy check; log them and deny.

### Proof test

1. Review: grep auth, middleware/proxy, Server Action and route handler code for `catch` blocks, and read each one on an auth or permission path.
Pass: every catch on those paths denies (401/403/redirect) or rethrows. Fail: any catch returns success, `true`, `next()` or the requested data.
2. Grep for `process.env.` used in comparisons (secrets, admin emails, feature flags).
Pass: each has a startup or in-place check that denies when the value is missing. Fail: an unset variable lets the comparison pass.
3. Optional, on a local or staging copy with a test account: unset one required secret, restart, and call a protected route. Pass: it refuses. Fail: it acts.

### Sources

- [OWASP Top 10 2025: A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A10_2025-Mishandling_of_Exceptional_Conditions/)
- [MITRE CWE-636: Not Failing Securely ('Failing Open')](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/636.html)

## API-17 Every live API route is known, documented and still needed

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1059 · Mode: review · Stacks: any, nextjs, vercel

### Risk

Old `/api/v1` routes, test and debug handlers, and endpoints left behind by a removed feature keep running with the checks they had when they were written. Nobody reviews them, so they miss newer auth and rate limits. Old preview deployments serve the same forgotten code (NEXT-14 covers their access).

### Build rule

Keep a short list of every route handler, Server Action module and edge function with its purpose, auth rule and owner (a table in the repo is enough). Delete routes that nothing calls. When a new version replaces a route, remove the old one or make it return 410. Remove debug and test endpoints before deploying.

### Proof test

1. List every `route.ts`/`route.js` under `app/`, every file under `pages/api/`, every `'use server'` module and every Supabase edge function.
2. Compare with the documented list.
Pass: every live route is documented with an auth rule, and every documented route exists. Fail: any undocumented, debug, test or superseded route is still deployed.
3. Check the production deployment's function list in the Vercel dashboard against the same list.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API9 Improper Inventory Management](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0xa9-improper-inventory-management/)

## API-18 Responses from third-party APIs are validated before use

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-20 · Mode: review · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

Server code often trusts what another API returns: it stores the fields as they come, follows redirects, renders HTML from them, or uses them in a database query. A compromised or spoofed provider, or one that changed its format, then injects data or code into your app. OWASP lists this as unsafe consumption of APIs.

### Build rule

Parse every third-party response with a schema (zod `safeParse`) and use only the parsed fields. Call providers over HTTPS only, with a timeout and a response size limit, and do not follow redirects to other hosts. Treat text from a provider as untrusted user input for rendering (BROWSER-09) and for queries. Verify webhook signatures (API-06) instead of trusting the payload.

### Proof test

1. Review: list every server-side `fetch` or SDK call to a third-party API.
2. For each, find where its response is used.
Pass: the response goes through a schema parse, and the call has a timeout and https URL. Fail: raw fields reach the database, HTML or a query, or the call has no timeout.
3. Optional, locally: point one provider URL at a stub that returns extra fields and a wrong type. Pass: the app rejects or ignores them.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs](https://api-security.owasp.org/editions/2023/en/0xaa-unsafe-consumption-of-apis/)

## API-19 No open redirects in redirect parameters

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-601 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any, nextjs, node

### Risk

A route that redirects to whatever a `next`, `returnTo`, `redirect` or `url` parameter says lets anyone build a link on the real domain that lands on their own site. Phishing mails use such links because the domain looks trusted, and in OAuth and magic-link flows an open redirect can hand an access token or code to the attacker.

### Build rule

Only redirect to relative paths: accept a value that starts with a single `/` and not `//` or `/\`, then build the URL from your own origin. If other hosts are needed, compare the parsed host against an exact allowlist. In Next.js, validate the parameter before calling `redirect()` or `NextResponse.redirect()`; fall back to `/` when the check fails.

### Proof test

1. The tool crawls the site and collects query parameters on same-origin links whose names look like redirect targets (next, url, continue, goto, redirect..., return..., dest..., callback_url).
2. For up to 8 of them it sends a GET per probe form of the same reserved host, `asa-redirect-probe.invalid` (it never resolves): `https://asa-redirect-probe.invalid/`, `//asa-redirect-probe.invalid/`, `/\asa-redirect-probe.invalid/`, `https:asa-redirect-probe.invalid/` and the double-encoded `%2F%2Fasa-redirect-probe.invalid%2F`. It stops at the first hit and never follows a redirect.
3. Fail: the `Location` header, a `Refresh` header or a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` tag sends the browser to `asa-redirect-probe.invalid`, read the way browsers read URLs (a backslash counts as a slash). Pass: every probe form stays on-site or does not redirect. Not applicable when no such parameter is linked; then test the login and logout redirects by hand the same way. Redirects done in JavaScript are not covered.

### Sources

- [OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html)

## API-20 No directory listings

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-548 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

When the web server lists the contents of a folder that has no index page, anyone can browse every file stored there, including uploads, exports and backups that were never linked.

### Build rule

Turn automatic indexes off: `autoindex off;` in nginx, `Options -Indexes` in Apache, no `directory` listing in static file middleware. Keep user uploads in object storage with private buckets and signed URLs rather than in a web-served folder.

### Proof test

1. The tool requests a few common folders (`/uploads/`, `/static/`, `/assets/`, `/images/`, `/files/`, `/backup/`, `/public/`) and the folders of same-origin files found by the crawl, up to 10 in total.
2. Fail: a 200 response is a server-generated index (`Index of /...` or `Directory listing for /...`). File names are not shown in the report.
3. Pass: none of them is a listing.

### Sources

- [CWE-548: Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/548.html)
- [nginx ngx_http_autoindex_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_autoindex_module.html)
- [Apache HTTP Server core: Options directive](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/core.html)

## API-21 No public debug or status endpoints

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-489, CWE-215 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Server and framework debug pages left reachable in production publish what an attacker would otherwise have to guess: Apache `server-status` shows live request URLs and client addresses, `phpinfo()` and Spring Boot's `/actuator/env` print configuration and environment values, and profilers expose request data and internals.

### Build rule

Do not deploy debug tools to production. Restrict Apache `mod_status` and `mod_info` to localhost, delete `phpinfo()` files, expose only `health` from Spring Boot Actuator (`management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health`) and put any other management endpoint on an internal port behind authentication.

### Proof test

1. The tool requests `/server-status`, `/server-info`, `/phpinfo.php`, `/info.php`, `/actuator/env`, `/debug/pprof/`, `/elmah.axd` and `/_profiler/` once each.
2. Fail: a 200 response whose content matches the real page (for example the Apache status heading, a `phpinfo()` title, or actuator JSON with `propertySources`). A single-page-app fallback page does not count. Contents are never shown.
3. Pass: none of them is served.

### Sources

- [Apache HTTP Server mod_status](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/mod_status.html)
- [Spring Boot reference: Actuator endpoints](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/actuator/endpoints.html)
- [PHP manual: phpinfo](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.phpinfo.php)
- [CWE-489: Active Debug Code](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/489.html)

## API-22 API description not public unless intended

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any, node

### Risk

A public OpenAPI or Swagger document lists every endpoint, parameter and model, including internal and admin routes that nothing in the UI links to. It does not create a flaw by itself, but it removes the guesswork from finding one, and old or forgotten endpoints show up in it.

### Build rule

Publish the API description only for APIs that are public by design. Otherwise serve it only in development or behind authentication, and keep it in sync with the deployed routes so that retired versions are actually removed.

### Proof test

1. The tool requests `/openapi.json`, `/swagger.json`, `/v3/api-docs`, `/api-docs`, `/swagger/v1/swagger.json`, `/api/openapi.json` and `/swagger-ui.html` once each.
2. Warning: a JSON document with an `openapi` or `swagger` field and a `paths` object, or a Swagger UI page, is served. Only the version and path count are reported.
3. Pass: none of them is served. Decide whether a warning is intended; if the API is public, record that and move on.

### Sources

- [OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API9 Improper Inventory Management](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa9-improper-inventory-management/)

## API-23 GraphQL introspection off in production

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any, node

### Risk

With introspection on, anyone can download the whole GraphQL schema: every query, mutation, type and field, including admin and internal ones. Attackers use it to find fields that resolvers forgot to protect. It is a warning, not a flaw by itself, because some APIs are public by design.

### Build rule

Disable introspection in production (for example `introspection: false` in Apollo Server, or a validation rule that rejects `__schema` and `__type`), keep it on in development, and still check authorization in every resolver, because hiding the schema is not access control.

### Proof test

1. The tool sends one POST to `/graphql` and `/api/graphql` with the standard, read-only introspection query `{ __schema { queryType { name } mutationType { name } types { name } } }`. It runs no resolvers and changes nothing.
2. Warning: the response contains `data.__schema`. Only the number of types and whether mutations exist are reported.
3. Pass: the answer is provably GraphQL and refuses: a GraphQL media type (`application/graphql-response+json`), or an error that names introspection, `__schema`, `__type`, "Cannot query field" or a `GRAPHQL_*` code. A generic JSON `{"errors": [...]}` proves nothing: it is manual when the status is not 404/405, and not applicable (no GraphQL endpoint) when it is.

### Sources

- [OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/GraphQL_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [GraphQL specification: Introspection](https://spec.graphql.org/October2021/)

## API-24 TRACE method disabled

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

A server that answers TRACE echoes the whole request back, headers included. Combined with another bug it can reveal cookies or authorization headers that a proxy adds (cross-site tracing), and it shows the server has not been hardened. Browsers no longer let pages send TRACE, so the risk is low.

### Build rule

Turn TRACE off: `TraceEnable off` in Apache, and in other servers and proxies allow only the methods the app uses (GET, HEAD, POST and the ones your API needs).

### Proof test

1. The tool sends one `TRACE /` request with a random `X-Asa-Trace-Probe` header.
2. Fail: the response is 200 and its body echoes the request line and the probe header.
3. Pass: any other answer (405, 501, or a normal page without the echo).

### Sources

- [OWASP WSTG: Test HTTP Methods](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing/06-Test_HTTP_Methods)
- [RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics (TRACE)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [Apache HTTP Server core: TraceEnable](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/core.html)

## API-30 No eval, new Function or vm on dynamic strings

Severity: critical · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-95 · Mode: review (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any, node, nextjs

### Risk

`eval`, `new Function`, Node's `vm` module and Python's `eval`/`exec` run a string as code with the server's rights. If any part of that string comes from a request, a stored record or a third-party response, an attacker runs their own code on the server and reads every secret it holds. `vm` is not a security sandbox.

### Build rule

Never turn data into code. Parse JSON with `JSON.parse`, look up handlers in a fixed map (`handlers[name]` with an allow list) instead of building function names, and use a real expression parser for formulas. Keep the CSP free of `'unsafe-eval'` so the browser refuses it too.

### Proof test

1. Run `asa code <path>`: it lists every `eval(`, `new Function(`, `vm.run*` and Python `eval`/`exec` call whose argument is not a string literal, with file and line.
Pass: none. Fail: any listed call. For each, trace where the string comes from; if it cannot contain request data, replace the call anyway and record why.
2. Confirm the deployed CSP has no `'unsafe-eval'` (BROWSER-02).

### Sources

- [CWE-95: Eval Injection](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html)
- [OWASP Node.js Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Nodejs_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## API-31 Shell commands never built from strings

Severity: critical · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-78 · Mode: review (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any, node, nextjs

### Risk

`child_process.exec`, `execSync`, `spawn` with `shell: true`, `os.system` and `subprocess` with `shell=True` hand the whole string to a shell. A value with `;`, `|`, backticks or `$( )` in it, such as a file name or a URL from a form, runs its own command on the server.

### Build rule

Do not call a shell. Use `execFile` or `spawn` with the program and an array of arguments (`shell: false`, the default), or Python `subprocess.run([...])` without `shell=True`. Validate arguments against an allow list, and put `--` before any value that could start with a dash.

### Proof test

1. Run `asa code <path>`: it lists every `exec`/`execSync` call whose command is built with a template string or `+`, every `shell: true`, and Python `os.system`/`subprocess` calls that use a shell with formatted strings.
Pass: none. Fail: any listed call; rewrite it with an argument array.

### Sources

- [CWE-78: OS Command Injection](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html)
- [OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## API-32 SQL is parameterized, never built by string concatenation

Severity: critical · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-89 · Mode: review (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any, node, nextjs, supabase

### Risk

A query built by pasting values into SQL text (a template string with `${}`, `+`, a Python f-string or `%`) lets a quote in the value end the string and add its own SQL. The attacker then reads or changes any table the database user can reach, and on Supabase the server often connects as a role that bypasses row-level security.

### Build rule

Pass values as parameters: `$1`/`?` placeholders with a values array, tagged templates that parameterize (the `sql` tag of postgres.js or drizzle, Prisma `$queryRaw` used as a tag), or the query builder. Never use `$queryRawUnsafe`, `sql.unsafe` or `knex.raw` with interpolated input. Table and column names that must vary come from a fixed allow list.

### Proof test

1. Run `asa code <path>`: it lists SQL text built from interpolated values or concatenation, and whether it is passed straight to a query call.
Pass: none. Fail: any query built from strings; warn: SQL-shaped strings with interpolation in files that run queries, to confirm by reading.

### Sources

- [CWE-89: SQL Injection](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html)
- [OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Query_Parameterization_Cheat_Sheet.html)
